title: Inside a black hole? What the sources predict—and why our sky test closed

visual_language.motion: slow diagram construction and state transitions only; no decorative particle fields

cards.heading: This route closed because it had no calibrated, identifying sky test
cards.narration: Could our universe be inside a black hole? This is Duho's personal interest, not a NebulaMind research frontier. We read the primary sources to ask what these ideas predict. Here is the verdict. One branch gives pulsars a number to check. But our galaxy-spin route cannot identify a black-hole origin: it has no calibrated target, and other rotating cosmologies can give the same broad signal. This closes one route. It does not say the idea is true or false.
cards.diagram: Three-column verdict map. Left: PERSONAL INTEREST badge above a plain nested-horizon icon, immediately paired with NOT A NEBULAMIND FRONTIER. Centre: PRIMARY SOURCES flow into two branches. Right branch A: PULSAR MASS -> CHECKABLE NUMBER. Right branch B: GALAXY SPIN -> NO CALIBRATED TARGET + SHARED SIGNAL -> ROUTE CLOSED. Animate branches by 8 seconds and hold the final map before 30 seconds.
on_screen_support: PERSONAL INTEREST · NOT A RESEARCH FRONTIER
GALAXY SPIN: NO CALIBRATED, IDENTIFYING TARGET
ROUTE CLOSED · IDEA NOT DECLARED TRUE OR FALSE

cards.heading: “Black-hole universe” names different programmes, not one model
cards.narration: The first surprise is structural. Lana found at least five different programmes under this label. One identifies a closed universe with a black hole. Another adds a torsion-driven bounce. Another inherits rotation. Cosmological natural selection asks whether black-hole production shapes physical constants. Other baby-universe work points to different observables. They do not share one forecast.
cards.diagram: One BHU label at upper left fans into five compact programme tiles. Each tile shows a distinct mechanism/observable glyph and a one-line label. Their output arrows terminate at different endpoints instead of converging. Do not use a cosmic montage.
on_screen_support: AT LEAST FIVE PROGRAMMES IN THIS SURVEY

cards.heading: A test needs a target that can be wrong—and that rivals do not share
cards.narration: To test an idea, the model has to risk being wrong. It needs a number, a range, or a distinctive pattern that a measurement can miss. And that target has to distinguish the model from its rivals. Lana found one clean numerical test in the family she surveyed. It does not use galaxy spins. It uses neutron stars.
cards.diagram: Build the central logic that will recur later: MODEL -> TARGET BAND -> MEASUREMENT. A second model points at the same target band and triggers NOT IDENTIFYING. Then switch to a unique target and show IDENTIFYING TEST. This is the key explanatory animation, fully local and deterministic.
on_screen_support: RIVALS MUST NOT SHARE THE SAME TARGET

cards.heading: Cosmological natural selection puts a low ceiling on neutron-star mass
cards.narration: In cosmological natural selection, universes reproduce through black holes with slightly changed constants. Those constants should sit near values that favour black-hole production. In the Brown–Lee–Rho chain Lana surveyed, the Brown–Bethe maximum neutron-star mass is about one point five solar masses. Their paper says a neutron star at approximately two solar masses or above would put that chain in “serious doubt or simply falsify” it. That is a real, falsifiable number.
cards.diagram: A restrained lineage diagram: universe -> black holes -> child universes with small parameter shifts. Transition to a horizontal neutron-star mass axis. Mark ~1.5 solar masses as Brown–Bethe maximum and shade the approximate >=2 solar-mass source regime with the exact quoted consequence SERIOUS DOUBT OR SIMPLY FALSIFY. No unsupported equation-of-state detail.
on_screen_support: “SERIOUS DOUBT OR SIMPLY FALSIFY” — BROWN, LEE & RHO

cards.heading: Measured pulsars have entered the source’s approximately two-solar-mass regime
cards.narration: Two pulsars reach the critical regime. Demorest's measurement is one point nine seven, plus or minus zero point zero four solar masses; its centre is below two. Fonseca's is two point zero eight, plus or minus zero point zero seven. The quoted sixty-eight point three percent interval stays above two. But the ninety-five point four percent lower bound is one point nine five. At that stronger credibility level, it does not clear two.
cards.diagram: Full, uncropped horizontal interval plot from 1.4 to 2.2 M☉. Draw the source's ~1.5 marker and the approximate 2 regime. Row 1: Demorest 1.97 ±0.04, central point below 2 and interval crossing. Row 2: Fonseca 2.08 ±0.07 at 68.3%, entirely above 2. Add a distinct 95.4% lower-bound arrow ending at 1.95. Label credibility levels directly; do not hide them in a legend.

cards.heading: The evidence enters the test regime; the packet does not call it falsification
cards.narration: This is where restraint matters. Brown, Lee, and Rho gave a disjunction: a heavy neutron star would put the chain in serious doubt, or simply falsify it. Lana's closing record does not decide which side applies, and neither will this video. The finding is narrower: observations have entered the regime named by the source.
cards.diagram: Keep the mass plot dimmed in the background. Place the exact source disjunction in two equal outlined boxes joined by OR. Stop a measurement arrow before either box and label PACKET DOES NOT ADJUDICATE. Highlight only ENTERS THE NAMED REGIME.

cards.heading: The rotating-parent source explicitly says the two handedness counts should differ
cards.narration: A different programme led to our sky work. If the parent black hole rotates, the child universe inherits its axis. The source says galaxies should tend to align with that axis. It then says clockwise- and counterclockwise-spinning galaxy counts should be different. The spin lane was not chasing a phantom. It followed an explicit, source-backed qualitative claim.
cards.diagram: Simple rotating-parent cross-section, axis line passing into a child-universe circle, then a field of stylized galaxy disks aligned around that axis. Split count bins CW and CCW with an unequal sign but no invented percentage. Footer: QUALITATIVE SOURCE CLAIM · NO AMPLITUDE SHOWN.

cards.heading: The handedness claim came after the cited data and never became a numerical forecast
cards.narration: But that sentence was added in 2025, after the galaxy studies cited as support. It was not a pre-data forecast. The paper gives rotating-frame mechanics, but not a numerical forecast for galaxy handedness: no expected size, no rule for how it changes with scale or redshift, no independently predicted direction, and no acceptance range for a new measurement.
cards.diagram: Timeline: cited galaxy observations appear first; 2025 revision and its unequal-count sentence appear later. Then a forecast contract form fills MECHANICS present but leaves four red outlined blanks: SIZE, SCALE/REDSHIFT LAW, INDEPENDENT DIRECTION, ACCEPTANCE RANGE. Avoid saying the source contains no numbers or equations.

cards.heading: A real spin difference would still not identify a black-hole origin
cards.narration: Suppose a controlled survey found a real spin-handedness difference. That would be interesting. But a positive generic anisotropy would not identify BHU. Other rotating cosmologies can lead to the same broad effect. One observed number would have more than one possible cause. A successful measurement is not automatically a successful test of this model.
cards.diagram: The centerpiece identifying-test diagram. Two plainly labelled source families—BHU ROTATING-PARENT and OTHER ROTATING COSMOLOGIES—both feed the same observed node CW/CCW DIFFERENCE. The observed node cannot route backward to a unique cause; animate the backward arrow splitting in two. Do not name specific rival models.

cards.heading: The spin route fails twice: no numerical target, and no unique signature
cards.narration: The route therefore fails in two independent ways. With no source-defined numerical range, neither a small result nor a finite-precision null can be scored. With no unique signature, a positive result cannot identify BHU. We could build a trustworthy measurement and still be unable to answer the BHU question. The hunt had a source. It did not have a target.
cards.diagram: Two-column fail-closed ledger. Column A: CALIBRATION—target range blank—cannot numerically score a finite result. Column B: IDENTIFICATION—two causes share one signal—cannot infer BHU. Both columns close into ROUTE CLOSED, while MEASUREMENT CAN STILL BE TRUSTWORTHY remains visibly separate.
on_screen_support: A TRUSTWORTHY NUMBER CAN STILL FAIL TO TEST BHU
THE HUNT HAD A SOURCE · IT DID NOT HAVE A TARGET

cards.heading: Reopen this route only for a calibrated target or a unique signature
cards.narration: What would change the verdict? First, a published calculation connecting parent-black-hole parameters to a handedness amplitude, scale, or redshift dependence, with a numerical acceptance region. Or second, a signature unique to birth behind a parent horizon, rather than a generic effect of rotation or a bounce. A confirmed spin asymmetry alone would still not test BHU. This route reopens only when a BHU model supplies a calibrated target or a unique signature.
cards.diagram: Return to the model-target-measurement diagram from card 03, now with two locked reopen gates: CALIBRATED TARGET and UNIQUE SIGNATURE. A standalone CONFIRMED SPIN ASYMMETRY token approaches but cannot unlock either gate. Finish with both requirements and the heading held alone long enough to read; no caveat or credit card follows.
on_screen_support: SPIN ASYMMETRY ALONE IS NOT A BHU TEST
